title: Tomorrow
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE PRESENT TENSE PLUS A TIME WORD IS THE FUTURE. Morgen arbeite ich is "tomorrow I'm working" — the same verb form that says "I work" today, with a time word in front of it. Nothing is added: no auxiliary, no second tense, no ending that moves. English reaches for "will" or "I'm going to" here, so the interference is a learner hunting for a helper verb that German does not want.

A FRONTED TIME WORD INVERTS THE CLAUSE, and this is M4's verb-second law reused rather than re-taught: the finite verb is the second ELEMENT, so when the time word takes first position the subject moves in behind the verb. Morgen esse ich Brot, never *Morgen ich esse Brot. An element can be one word or three — Am Wochenende is two words and one element — and the verb comes straight after it either way.

will IS NOT ENGLISH "will", and it is the sharpest false friend German has for an English speaker. Ich will Brot is the verb wollen and means "I want bread", said the blunt way a child says it. It is not a future at all: the future is the present-plus-time-word above, and the polite want is M3's Ich möchte. There is no German word standing where English "will" stands.

werden + infinitive (ich werde essen) is German's other future, and it is deliberately left for a later level. It carries prediction and emphasis — what you think will happen — not a plan already made, which is everything an L1 learner needs to say about tomorrow. Naming it here is what stops it being imported a level early.

möchte still takes a BARE infinitive at the end of the clause, and the time word simply slots in between: Ich möchte morgen Deutsch lernen. That is M3's clause bracket, unchanged — möchte second, lernen last — so the future costs the bracket nothing, and there is still no word for "to" inside it.

A DAY OR A STRETCH OF TIME TAKES am: am Montag, am Dienstag, am Freitag, am Wochenende. That is the same am M4 opened for time, the fusion of an and dem, and English's bare "on Monday" has nothing standing where it stands. Day names and Wochenende are nouns, so all of them are capitalised.

A QUESTION WORD IS THE FIRST ELEMENT, so the verb is still second and the subject follows it: Was machen Sie morgen? Wann kommen Sie morgen? German asks with word order alone — there is no do to insert, exactly as M2's yes/no questions had none.

words.note: tomorrow. Capitalised, Morgen is “morning”; lowercase it is “tomorrow”. Opening a sentence it is capitalised for position, not meaning — Morgen arbeite ich is “tomorrow”, filling the time slot.

sentences.trap: There is no future tense here to go looking for. The verb is the same arbeite the learner met in L1-M4 for "I work", and the only thing carrying "tomorrow" is the word morgen. Adding a helper verb to make it feel more like a future is what breaks it.
sentences.sound: MOR-gen, with a throaty r and a hard g at the back. arbeite is AR-bye-tuh: ei is "eye", and the r after the a barely sounds. ich is the soft hissed ch made at the front of the mouth — never the k of "ick".

variations.changed: L1-M3's nicht negating the verb, standing at the end where it belongs
a different verb in the same slot, with an object after the inverted pair; the shape and the tense do not move
the subject back in front, so nothing inverts — morgen can sit inside the sentence as well as in front of it

mistake.why: The time word has taken first position, so the verb must come second and the subject third: Morgen arbeite ich. Putting the subject back in front of the verb copies the English order, and it is the commonest slip in this module.

sentences.usage: Saying what you are doing tomorrow — the everyday German future, in a shop, at work, anywhere.
sentences.mnemonic: The time word goes first, so the verb hops over the subject to stay second.

sentences.cue: The day after tomorrow I'm going home

words.note: the day after tomorrow, in ONE word: über (“over”) stacked onto morgen. English needs four words; German welds them. One token, one word row, no claim on the morgen inside.
fahren — to go by car, train, bus or bike: ich fahre, Sie fahren. gehen is on foot, so a trip home from another town is fahren. English has one “go” for both; German asks how you are getting there.

sentences.trap: nach Hause is one fixed phrase meaning "home" as a destination, taken whole in L1-M5's Ich bin nach Hause gegangen. It never takes an article, and the bare nach on its own is written nowhere in this level. Two verbs go home: gehen on foot, fahren by anything with wheels — Übermorgen gehe ich nach Hause says you will walk there.
sentences.sound: ÜBER has the ü of pursed lips — say "ee" with your lips rounded. fahre is FAH-ruh: a long a, the h only lengthening it, and a final -e voiced as a weak uh. Hause is HOW-zuh: au is the ow of "how", and an s between vowels is a z.

variations.changed: one day nearer; the sentence is otherwise identical

variations.cue: The day after tomorrow I'm walking home
variations.changed: gehen instead of fahren: on foot — said when home is a walk away, not a train ride

variations.display: Übermorgen fahre ich früh nach Hause
variations.cue: The day after tomorrow I'm going home early
variations.changed: L1-M4's früh added; it sits before the destination, not after it

mistake.display: Übermorgen fahre ich nach dem Haus
mistake.why: The destination "home" is the frozen phrase nach Hause, with no article at all. nach dem Haus is an attempt at "to the house" and is not how anybody says they are going home.

sentences.usage: Fixing a return date two days out — the trip home, by train or by car.
sentences.mnemonic: über + morgen: one word past tomorrow.

words.note: what. It asks for a thing and takes first position, so the verb comes straight after and the subject follows. Nothing stands where English's do stands in “what DO you do”.
to do — and to make: one verb where English has two. The Sie form machen is spelled like the infinitive; the ich form is mache. M5's gemacht is its own row.

sentences.trap: English builds this question out of two verbs — "what DO you DO" — and German builds it out of none: was, then the verb, then Sie. A learner hunting for the German "do" is hunting for a word that does not exist.
sentences.sound: vahs — the German w is an English v, every time. machen has the throaty ch made at the back of the mouth, the one in Scottish "loch", and that is a different sound from the soft front ch of ich.

variations.cue: What are you doing on Monday?
variations.changed: a named day instead of tomorrow
a more specific verb in the same slot
the time word dropped — and with it the future reading; now it is about right now

mistake.why: The question word is the first element, so the verb has to be second: Was machen Sie morgen? Leaving the subject in front of the verb copies the English shape and puts the German verb in a slot it never occupies.

sentences.usage: Making a plan with somebody, or being asked to make one.
sentences.mnemonic: Question word, verb, subject — in that order, always.

words.note: to learn — and to study a language: ich lerne, Sie lernen, infinitive and Sie form one word. Same root as English “learn”. After möchte it goes to the end of the clause: Ich möchte Deutsch lernen.

sentences.trap: English says "I'm learning German tomorrow" or "I'll learn"; German says it in the plain present with morgen in front, and the fronting inverts: lerne before ich. With möchte the infinitive would go last — Ich möchte morgen Deutsch lernen — but without it there is no bracket, and lerne is simply the second element.
sentences.sound: LEHR-nuh — the r after the vowel barely sounds, closer to LEH-nuh than an English speaker expects. Deutsch is DOYTCH: eu is always "oy", and the tsch on the end is the ch of English "watch".

variations.cue: I'd like to learn German tomorrow
variations.changed: möchte added, so the infinitive goes to the END — L1-M3's bracket, with the time word inside it
today for tomorrow; the same present tense either way, and the same inversion
the subject in front, so no inversion — morgen drops into the middle instead

mistake.why: morgen has taken first position, so the verb must be second: Morgen lerne ich Deutsch. This is the slip S01 warned about, and it is worth catching twice — the English order is the strongest habit in the module.

sentences.usage: A plan announced rather than proposed — what tomorrow holds.
sentences.mnemonic: Time first, verb second — and with no möchte there is no bracket to close.

words.note: Tuesday. Every day name is a noun, so capitalised, and it takes am — am Dienstag, M4's contraction doing its time job. The ie is one long ee: DEENS-tahk.

sentences.trap: am Dienstag is TWO words and ONE element, so the verb still comes straight after it. Counting words instead of counting elements is what produces *Am Dienstag ich arbeite nicht.
sentences.sound: DEENS-tahk — the ie is one long ee sound, and the final -g of Tag hardens to a k. arbeite is AR-by-tuh, with the ei said like English "eye".

variations.changed: a different day, with am unchanged in front of it
nicht dropped — the plain positive, and the same inversion
a one-word time element instead of a two-word one, and it is about today — the verb sits in exactly the same slot

mistake.why: am Dienstag has taken first position, so arbeite must be second and ich third. The two words of the time phrase count as one element, not two.

sentences.usage: Telling a colleague or a shop when you are not around.
sentences.mnemonic: One element, however many words it took to say it.

sentences.display: Am Wochenende stehe ich spät auf
sentences.cue: At the weekend I get up late
sentences.literal: On-the weekend stand I late up

words.note: weekend — Woche and Ende welded into one capitalised noun, one token. It takes am like a day: am Wochenende. A compound's gender comes from its LAST part: das Wochenende, because Ende is neuter.

sentences.trap: Two things happen at once here and neither is new: the time phrase fronts and inverts the clause, and M4's separable prefix auf still flies to the very end. The prefix goes after spät, not before it — it is always the last thing in the clause.
sentences.sound: VO-khen-EN-duh, with the throaty ch of machen in the middle and a voiced final -e. stehe is SHTEH-uh: an initial st- is said sht- in German, always.

variations.display: Am Wochenende stehe ich früh auf
variations.cue: At the weekend I get up early
variations.changed: früh for spät; the prefix still closes the clause
a one-word time element, and the sentence is now about tomorrow

variations.cue: At the weekend I don't work
variations.changed: an ordinary verb with no prefix, so nothing has to travel to the end

mistake.display: Am Wochenende auf stehe ich spät
mistake.why: The prefix does not travel with the verb; it goes to the END of the clause and nowhere else: Am Wochenende stehe ich spät auf. Reassembling aufstehen in the middle of the sentence is exactly what M4 spent its module warning about.

sentences.usage: Explaining your weekend to somebody who wants to ring you at eight.
sentences.mnemonic: Time first, verb second, prefix dead last.

sentences.cue: Tomorrow I'd like to do nothing

words.note: nothing — one letter from M3's nicht (“not”). nicht denies a verb or adjective and never stands for a thing; nichts IS the thing and fills the object slot: Ich möchte nichts. Two keys, two jobs.

sentences.trap: nichts is an object, so it sits where an object sits — inside the bracket, before the infinitive. It does not behave like nicht, which chases the verb it is denying; the two words look alike and stand in different places for different reasons.
sentences.sound: NIKHTS with the soft front ch, the same sound as in ich, and a clean -ts on the end. That final s is the only audible difference from nicht, so it has to be said.

variations.cue: Today I'd like to do nothing
variations.changed: today instead of tomorrow; the same present tense either way

variations.cue: Tomorrow I don't want to work
variations.changed: nicht instead of nichts — now the working is denied rather than an empty object named

variations.display: Am Wochenende möchte ich nichts machen
variations.cue: At the weekend I'd like to do nothing
variations.changed: a two-word time element fronted; the bracket does not move

mistake.why: The infinitive closes the clause, so the object goes in front of it: nichts machen, not machen nichts. This is the English order again, and the bracket is what it breaks.

sentences.usage: Refusing a plan without giving a reason.
sentences.mnemonic: nicht denies; nichts is the empty thing itself.

words.note: today. Behaves exactly like morgen — a one-word time element that fronts and inverts — and shows that the verb does not change: one present tense covers today and tomorrow; the time word decides.
to buy. Regular: kaufe for ich, kaufen for Sie — the Sie form spelled like the infinitive, as with essen and kommen. M5's participle gekauft is its own row; this is the present.

sentences.trap: This sentence is the control: it is built exactly like Morgen arbeite ich and it is not about the future at all. That is the module's whole point — the German present says both, and the time word is the only thing that decides which.
sentences.sound: HOY-tuh — the German eu is the oy of "boy", never "ee-oo". kaufe has the au of "how": KOW-fuh.

variations.changed: one word swapped, and the sentence is now about the future — nothing else moves
a different thing bought
the subject fronted, so there is no inversion — heute drops into the middle instead

mistake.why: heute is the first element, so kaufe is second. The rule does not care that the time word is about today rather than tomorrow: it is about position, not about meaning.

sentences.usage: The everyday errand, said out loud.
sentences.mnemonic: Today and tomorrow share one tense; only the word in front changes.

words.note: Friday. A noun, so capitalised, and it takes am like every day. The ei is English “eye” — FRY-tahk. Keep it beside Dienstag: ei is “eye”, ie is “ee”, and German never swaps them.

later. A time word like morgen and heute — it can front and invert — but here it sits at the end, where a time adverb lands when something else holds first position. “Later”, not “late”: that is spät.

sentences.trap: später is a comparison and spät is a judgement. Ich komme später says only that it will be after the time first named; Ich komme spät says the hour itself is late. English blurs them and German does not.
sentences.sound: SHPAY-ter. An initial sp- is said shp-, the same rule that turns st- into sht-. The ä is the ay of "bay" with no glide at the end.

variations.changed: a different day in the same slot
a one-word time element fronted instead of a two-word one
früh for später — the opposite end of the day, and the same shape

mistake.why: Two words of time still make one element, so komme is second and ich comes after it. This is the same slip as *Am Dienstag ich arbeite nicht, and it is worth making twice.

sentences.usage: Warning a colleague or a host that you will not be there on the hour.
sentences.mnemonic: ei says eye, ie says ee — Freitag and Dienstag, side by side.

words.note: when — the ASKING one only. English uses one “when” to ask and to join; German splits them: wann only asks a question. The joining one is wenn (M10), a different spelling and a different key.

sentences.trap: wann is the question and wenn is the join. Reaching for wann inside a statement is the mistake this row exists to stop, and M10 is where the other half of the pair arrives.
sentences.sound: vahn — the w is a v, and the double n is one plain n. kommen has a short o and a clearly voiced final -en.

variations.changed: the time word dropped, so the question is about now rather than tomorrow
a different verb; wann still holds first position

variations.cue: When are you working on Monday?
variations.changed: a named day at the end, where a second time phrase can sit

mistake.why: wann is the first element, so the verb is second and Sie third: Wann kommen Sie morgen? German asks with word order and nothing else, so there is no do to hide the verb behind.

sentences.usage: Pinning down a time somebody has been vague about.
